name: Difelikefalin
route: IV injection into the dialysis line at the end of each hemodialysis session
status: FDA-approved (2021) for moderate-to-severe itch from chronic kidney disease in adults on hemodialysis
mechanism: Activates kappa-opioid receptors on nerves and immune cells outside the brain, damping itch signals without the euphoria of brain-acting opioids
uses: Itch from chronic kidney disease in adults on hemodialysis

article.summary: Difelikefalin (Korsuva) is an IV peptide given after hemodialysis to relieve moderate-to-severe itch caused by chronic kidney disease. FDA-approved in 2021.
article.takeaway: Difelikefalin is a small synthetic peptide that activates kappa-opioid receptors, which help regulate itch, while staying largely outside the brain. It was the first FDA-approved treatment for **itch linked to chronic kidney disease** in people on hemodialysis, a common and often sleep-wrecking symptom. In phase 3 trials, about half of treated patients had a clinically meaningful drop in itch, compared with about a third on placebo.[^1][^2] It is injected into the dialysis line three times a week, so there is nothing to take at home.[^3] Dizziness, sleepiness and diarrhea are the main side effects, and it is not a controlled substance.
glance: Moderate-to-severe CKD-associated itch in adults on hemodialysis
IV bolus into the dialysis circuit at the end of each session, usually three times a week
Two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials (KALM-1 and KALM-2) with 851 participants

blocks.text: Kidney failure leaves many people with persistent, often whole-body itch. Its causes are not fully understood, but an imbalance in the body's opioid signaling appears to play a part: activity at mu-opioid receptors tends to promote itch, while kappa-opioid receptors tend to suppress it.

Difelikefalin is built from D-amino acids, mirror-image building blocks that resist breakdown, and it is water-loving enough that little of it crosses into the brain. It switches on kappa-opioid receptors on sensory nerve endings and immune cells in the skin and body, turning down itch signals at their source. Because it does not act on the brain's mu-opioid reward pathways, it was not expected to cause euphoria or dependence, and it is not scheduled by the DEA.[^3]

rows: 378 U.S. adults on hemodialysis with moderate-to-severe itch
At least a 3-point itch drop (0-10 scale) in 49.1% vs 27.9% on placebo[^1]
851 adults in North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific
3-point drop in 51.1% vs 35.2%; 4-point drop in 38.7% vs 23.4%[^2]

blocks.text: Patients also reported better itch-related quality of life, and benefit began within the first week and held through an open-label extension of up to 64 weeks.[^2] The placebo response was substantial, which is typical of itch studies.

The dose is 0.5 micrograms per kilogram of body weight, given by the dialysis team as a quick injection into the venous line of the dialysis circuit at the end of each session. If a session is missed, the dose is simply given after the next one. It has not been studied in people on peritoneal dialysis and is not recommended for them.[^3]

items: **Most common:** diarrhea (9% vs 6% on placebo), dizziness, nausea, unsteady walking, headache and high potassium[^3]

**Nervous system:** sleepiness, confusion and falls; sleepiness was more common in people 65 and older (7% vs about 3%), and sedatives, sedating antihistamines or opioid pain medicines can add to these effects[^3]
**Daily life:** the label advises caution with driving or operating machinery until the effect on alertness is known[^3]

blocks.text: It is not recommended for people with severe liver impairment, and human data in pregnancy are too limited to judge the risk.

Korsuva was approved in August 2021 for adults on hemodialysis. An oral version was studied for other itchy conditions: it modestly reduced itch in a phase 2 trial in notalgia paresthetica, an itchy patch on the upper back,[^4] but the developer ended that program in 2024 after a larger dose-finding study showed no meaningful benefit over placebo.[^5] No oral form is approved.

evidence.label: Strong: two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials
evidence.text: Two randomized phase 3 trials with 851 participants showed consistent, moderate itch relief over placebo.[^1][^2] The effect is real but not universal: roughly half of treated patients reached a meaningful improvement.

faq.q: Is difelikefalin an opioid? Can it be addictive?
faq.a: It acts on kappa-opioid receptors, a different branch of the opioid system from morphine-like drugs, and it mostly stays out of the brain. It is not a controlled substance.[^3]
In the pooled trials, itch scores began separating from placebo within the first week.[^2]

faq.q: Can I use it if I'm on peritoneal dialysis or not on dialysis?
faq.a: It is approved only for adults on hemodialysis. It has not been studied in peritoneal dialysis, and no version is approved for people with kidney disease who are not on dialysis.[^3]
